_link.title: I can explain rerouting as a mechanism of synaptic plasticity

toLevel2.stem: What is rerouting in the context of synaptic plasticity?
toLevel2.answer: Forming a new connection with an undamaged neuron after damage
distractors: Growing new dendritic branches to increase neural reach
Removing unused synaptic connections between two neurons
Strengthening existing connections through repeated use

toLevel2.stem: What happens to the original connection during rerouting?
toLevel2.answer: The neuron abandons the connection to the damaged neuron
distractors: The original connection is strengthened and maintained
The damaged neuron repairs itself and reconnects fully
Both the original and new connections remain active

toLevel2.stem: What is the primary outcome of rerouting?
toLevel2.answer: Brain functioning is restored via an alternative route
distractors: New neurons are created to replace damaged neurons
The damaged neural pathway is permanently eliminated
All connections in the area are removed by pruning

toLevel2.stem: Rerouting is one of three mechanisms of synaptic plasticity. What are the other two?
distractors: LTP and LTD only
Excitation and inhibition
Myelination and transmission

toLevel2.stem: How does rerouting differ from sprouting?
toLevel2.answer: Rerouting redirects existing connections; sprouting grows new ones
distractors: Rerouting grows new branches; sprouting redirects connections
Rerouting removes connections; sprouting also removes them
Rerouting and sprouting are identical mechanisms of plasticity

toLevel2.stem: Rerouting involves a neuron abandoning a connection to a damaged neuron and forming a new connection with an undamaged neuron.
distractors: False

toLevel2.stem: Rerouting is the same as sprouting because both involve forming new neural connections.
distractors: True

toLevel2.stem: Rerouting occurs when a neuron connected to a {{blank:1}} neuron abandons that connection and forms a new one with an undamaged neuron.

distractors: healthy

toLevel2.stem: Rerouting restores brain functioning by establishing a synaptic connection via an {{blank:1}} route.

distractors: identical
temporary

toLevel2.stem: The three mechanisms of synaptic plasticity are sprouting, {{blank:1}}, and pruning.

distractors: inhibition
potentiation

toLevel3.stem: Why is rerouting particularly important after brain injury?
toLevel3.answer: It allows alternative pathways to restore lost functions
distractors: It repairs the damaged neurons to their original state
It removes the damaged neurons to prevent further harm
It creates entirely new neurons to replace damaged ones

toLevel3.stem: How does rerouting differ from pruning?
toLevel3.answer: Rerouting redirects connections; pruning removes unused ones
distractors: Rerouting removes connections; pruning redirects them instead
Both rerouting and pruning serve the same function exactly
Rerouting adds new growth; pruning adds different new growth

toLevel3.stem: Why does recovery through rerouting often result in only partial restoration of function?
toLevel3.answer: Alternative connections may not replicate the original pathway exactly
distractors: Rerouting can only occur in the first week after brain injury happens
Undamaged neurons are always weaker than the original damaged neurons
Rerouting is a temporary process that reverses itself after recovery

toLevel3.stem: What distinguishes rerouting from sprouting when both involve forming new connections?
toLevel3.answer: Rerouting replaces a lost connection; sprouting adds entirely new ones
distractors: Sprouting replaces a lost connection; rerouting adds new ones instead
Rerouting occurs only during learning; sprouting occurs only after injury
There is no meaningful distinction between rerouting and sprouting

toLevel3.stem: Why is rerouting described as establishing a connection via an 'alternative route'?
toLevel3.answer: The signal reaches its destination through a different neuron
distractors: The signal travels faster by taking a shorter neural pathway
The original pathway is repaired and used in a different way
The damaged neuron recovers and the route returns to normal

toLevel3.stem: How does rehabilitation support the process of rerouting after brain injury?
toLevel3.answer: Repeated activity encourages formation of alternative neural pathways
distractors: Rehabilitation repairs the original damaged neurons directly
Rehabilitation prevents rerouting from occurring too quickly
Rehabilitation has no influence on rerouting or neural recovery

toLevel3.stem: Rerouting explains how the brain can partially recover function after injury by finding alternative neural pathways.
distractors: False

toLevel3.stem: Rerouting differs from sprouting because rerouting {{blank:1}} an existing lost connection, while sprouting creates entirely {{blank:2}} connections.

distractors: strengthens
eliminates

distractors: complete

toLevel3.stem: Rehabilitation supports rerouting by encouraging the formation of {{blank:1}} neural pathways through repeated activity.

distractors: identical

toLevel4.stem: After a stroke damages neurons in Marcus's motor pathway, he gradually regains some ability to move his left hand over weeks of rehabilitation. Which mechanism best explains this recovery?
toLevel4.answer: Rerouting formed alternative connections around the damaged area
distractors: The damaged neurons fully regenerated to their original state
Pruning removed the damaged neurons and replaced them entirely
New neurons were created to take over the damaged pathway exactly

toLevel4.stem: A patient who suffered brain damage to their speech area can now speak using slightly different phrasing after months of therapy. Which mechanism of synaptic plasticity best accounts for this?
toLevel4.answer: Rerouting directed signals through alternative neural pathways
distractors: Pruning removed the speech pathways that were not damaged
Sprouting eliminated the connections to the damaged regions
LTD weakened the connections that were causing the difficulty

toLevel4.stem: A neuroscientist observes that after injury, a neuron that was connected to a damaged neuron now connects to a nearby undamaged neuron. Which mechanism is illustrated?
distractors: Sprouting
Pruning
Potentiation

toLevel4.stem: Ella's teacher asks her to distinguish between rerouting and sprouting in a brain injury scenario. Which response is correct?
toLevel4.answer: Rerouting redirects to undamaged neurons; sprouting grows new branches
distractors: Rerouting grows new branches; sprouting redirects existing connections
Both rerouting and sprouting involve removing unused neural connections
Rerouting and sprouting are the same process with different names only

toLevel4.stem: A VCE exam scenario describes a patient whose vision partially recovered after injury to the visual cortex. Which mechanism best explains the partial recovery?
toLevel4.answer: Rerouting established alternative pathways for visual processing
distractors: Pruning removed the damaged visual neurons to allow regrowth
The damaged neurons fully repaired themselves over several weeks
New visual neurons were generated to replace the damaged cells

toLevel4.stem: A physiotherapist explains to a patient that repeated exercises will help their brain 'find new ways' to control their injured leg. Which mechanism is the physiotherapist describing?
distractors: Pruning of the motor pathways
LTD of the damaged connections
Inhibition of the motor neurons

toLevel4.stem: Jake reads that rerouting can occur after a traumatic brain injury. He asks why recovery is often incomplete. Which explanation best applies?
toLevel4.answer: Alternative pathways may not fully replicate the original ones
distractors: Rerouting can only occur in children under the age of ten years
The brain stops all plasticity mechanisms after an injury occurs
Rerouting always produces complete and permanent recovery from injury

toLevel4.stem: After Marcus's stroke, {{blank:1}} allowed neighbouring undamaged neurons to form alternative connections that partially restored his ability to move.

distractors: pruning
inhibition

toLevel4.stem: A physiotherapist encourages repeated exercises to promote {{blank:1}}, which helps the brain establish alternative pathways around damaged areas.

distractors: pruning
inhibition

toLevel4.stem: Recovery after brain injury through rerouting is often only {{blank:1}} because the alternative connections may not function identically to the original ones.

distractors: complete
immediate

toLevel5.stem: A student claims that rerouting can fully restore all brain functions lost after a major injury. Which evaluation is most accurate?
toLevel5.answer: Unlikely; rerouting typically produces only partial recovery
distractors: Correct; rerouting always restores complete brain functioning
Correct; alternative pathways are identical to original ones
Incorrect; rerouting cannot restore any function at all ever

toLevel5.stem: Dr Singh argues that rerouting and sprouting are the same mechanism because both create new connections. Which evaluation is most justified?
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect; rerouting replaces lost connections while sprouting adds new ones
distractors: Correct; both mechanisms create connections and are therefore identical
Correct; the distinction between them is purely academic and unnecessary
Incorrect; neither mechanism actually creates any new connections at all

toLevel5.stem: A student argues that rerouting makes rehabilitation unnecessary because the brain will automatically find new pathways. Which evaluation is most accurate?
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect; rehabilitation supports and promotes the rerouting process
distractors: Correct; the brain reroutes without any external intervention needed
Correct; rehabilitation has no effect on the process of neural rerouting
Incorrect; rehabilitation prevents rerouting from occurring in the brain

toLevel5.stem: Emma claims that rerouting only occurs after physical brain injury, not during normal learning. Which evaluation is most justified?
toLevel5.answer: Rerouting is primarily associated with injury recovery at VCE level
distractors: Incorrect; rerouting is the primary mechanism of all daily learning
Correct; but rerouting also never occurs after injury in any case
Incorrect; rerouting has no connection to brain injury or recovery

toLevel5.stem: A student writes that rerouting involves repairing the damaged neuron. Which evaluation is most accurate?
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect; rerouting bypasses the damaged neuron via an alternative connection
distractors: Correct; rerouting repairs the damaged neuron to its original state
Correct; the damaged neuron is always fully restored during rerouting
Incorrect; rerouting removes the damaged neuron from the brain entirely

toLevel5.stem: Marcus argues that pruning would be more useful than rerouting after brain injury because removing damaged connections is simpler. Which evaluation is most justified?
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect; rerouting restores function while pruning only removes connections
distractors: Correct; pruning is always more effective than rerouting after any injury
Correct; removing damaged connections automatically restores brain function
Incorrect; pruning and rerouting serve exactly the same function after injury

toLevel5.stem: A researcher claims that rerouting is instantaneous and occurs immediately after brain injury. Which evaluation is most accurate?
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect; rerouting occurs gradually, often over weeks of rehabilitation
distractors: Correct; rerouting happens immediately to protect the brain from damage
Correct; all synaptic plasticity mechanisms occur instantaneously always
Incorrect; rerouting cannot begin until at least one year after an injury

toLevel5.stem: A student suggests that rerouting is less important than sprouting because it only redirects existing signals. Which evaluation is most justified?
toLevel5.answer: Both are essential; rerouting uniquely restores lost connections after damage
distractors: Correct; rerouting is a minor mechanism with little practical importance
Correct; sprouting can fully replace the need for rerouting in all cases
Incorrect; rerouting is the only mechanism of plasticity that truly matters
